about.title: About
about.content:
PZ: These are notes based on personal experience with a Shima Seiki MACH2XS153-15L and MACH2X M173X15L, and passing experience with shaping machines (SVR123SP, SES122S, SCG122SN), a Mini machine (SWG091N2), and a Kniterate. And some needle knitting and loom knitting experience. Therefore, the notes will have certain biases.
Big thanks to:

The people in my workplaces (past and present) who taught me what they know about textiles and worked to create a conducive environment for textile exploration.
The Shima Seiki technicians and trainers, and the salespeople and administrators who make access to the technicians and trainers possible.
Other people in the industry and research community who shared insights, contacts, time, and care.
People whom I’ve never met who created documentation for the unknown person who might benefit from them.
YH, for introducing the SUTD knitting researchers to Obsidian, developing the irobango plugin, sorting out Quartz, and explaining how to put this on the Internet. (And Claude.ai for giving me the dummies guide on how to download Node.js and use GitHub.)

mach2x/automatic-software.title: Automatic Software
mach2x/automatic-software.content:
Also called New File Format?
If you used the Automatic Software and want to go back to the older, Create Page software, but KnitPaint seems stuck in Automatic Software mode, if I remember correctly, Tat Lin found that uploading a QFD file for an old file format into Automatic Software Settings will get KnitPaint to return to the old file format mode.
We’ll try this out in person.

mach2x/carriage-systems.title: Carriage Systems
mach2x/carriage-systems.content:
The MACH2X carriage has 3 systems for each needle bed. The middle system is a knitting (K) system, while the left and right systems are transfer (T) systems.
Unlike shaping machines, each system cannot do both knitting and transfer. And since there is only 1 knitting system, the carriage can move only 1 yarn carrier at a time, though the carriage can pick up and drop multiple non-overlapping yarn carriers in a single carriage movement.
The lead transfer system is numbered S1, the middle knitting system is numbered S2, and the tail transfer system is numbered S3. So, the left-side transfer system may be either S1 or S3, depending on the direction of carriage movement.

Diagram showing systems for the front needle beds. Purple: transfer systems. Yellow: knitting systems.
Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Lecture Help > 4. Action of Each Part on Machine > System.

mach2x/comb.title: Comb
mach2x/comb.content:
The comb force is specified in kg. The comb force is scaled to the width of the knitted fabric. The scaling is determined based on the following parameters:

Minimum comb force: Comb force at Needle Min.
Maximum comb force: Comb force at Needle Max.
Needle min.
Needle max.

The comb force is interpolated linearly between the Min and Max values.

If you need to specify an exact comb force, set the Min and Max comb force to the same value so that the comb force does not vary with the fabric width.
Suggested settings
Suggested comb force settings for MACH2X M173X15L. Note that the settings will change depending on the yarn, the mood of the machine, and the alignment of the moon and the stars. Take the settings below as a starting point and adjust based on what you see on the machine.













































Fabric width (pitch)Comb force =2 (when comb grabs elastic setup yarn)Comb force =3100-360p6-12kg7.5-14kg90p6-12kg7.5-14kg  (actual: 8kg)80p6-12kg6.4-12kg (actual: 6.8kg)70p5.2-10kg5.2-10kg (actual: 5.5kg)60p4-9kg4-9kg  (actual: 4.2-4.3kg)50p3-8kg  (actual: 3.2kg)4-8kg (actual: 4.2kg)40pHaven’t been able to find a setting that works
Settings assume that Needle Min = 1, Needle Max = 1020.
For L10/L11=2, which is used when the comb grabs the SSUPY (elastic yarn at the start), don’t make the comb force too low, otherwise the comb will hang. On the MACH2XS153-15L, a comb force of less than 3kg can result in a comb hang, even if the fabric width is narrow.
PDOWN %
At the start of the knit, the comb will rise to grab the SSUPY/elastic setup yarn. After the comb has descended beyond the pulldown device (PDD), which is usually after about 80-90 courses of waste yarn, the PDD will be activated. To avoid breakage from the force of the comb plus the PDD, the comb force can be scaled down using PDOWN %. This is typically set to 80% so that the comb force is adjusted to 80% of its specified value after the PDD are activated.
Narrow fabrics
Finding the optimal comb force setting is more difficult for narrower fabrics. The lack of sinkers on the MACH2X may also make it more difficult to find feasible takedown settings. On the MACH2XS153-15L, I recall that we could knit 40p wide fabrics, and potentially even 16p wide fabrics.
It is possible to Auto Process 32p-wide fabric using the No Waste yarn-in setting in Automatic Software Settings.
It is possible to Auto Process 16p-wide fabric using the Standard yarn-in setting in Automatic Software Settings.
Why use waste knitting to release the comb
Knitting is less reliable when the comb is active because the fabric is held in a stretched state course-wise/horizontally. This makes knitting difficult, especially for some types of yarn.
When the comb releases, the fabric is more relaxed in the course-wise direction and knitting is more reliable.
Knit about 130-150 courses of waste yarn to release the comb.

mach2x/comparison-between-mach2x-and-oth.filePath: MACH2X/Comparison Between MACH2X and Other Shima Seiki Machines.md
mach2x/comparison-between-mach2x-and-oth.title: Comparison Between MACH2X and Other Shima Seiki Machines
mach2x/comparison-between-mach2x-and-oth.content:
Note that all these claims are based on my fairly limited experience with Shima Seiki knitting machines.
Advantage of machines with 4 needle beds (X-bed):

Can knit full gauge knit structures that require both front and back needle beds (e.g., tubular structures, double-layer fabrics) and transfers (e.g., inside shaping, knit structures that require back knits on the front bed/front knits on the back bed).

Some other Shima Seiki knitting machines, such as the SWG091N2 (Mini) have transfer needles. Transfer needles can be used to transfer loops to create full gauge patterns with inside shaping. However, transfer needles cannot knit, so the transfer needles cannot be used to knit structures that require back knits on the front body, and vice versa.



Limitations of Shima Seiki MACH2X/MACH2XS:

Cannot knit all-needle structures such as all-needle 1×1 rib.
Cannot tuck on upper needle beds.
Produces unreliable plating results, even with the RP carrier.
Carriage systems cannot do both knit and transfer. Each system can either knit or transfer.

Note that there are different stitch pressers (STP) for knitting and transfer systems. Mixing them up can damage the loop pressers.


Cannot move more than 1 yarn carrier at a time because there is only 1 knitting system.

Yarn carriers on different parts of the needle bed can be picked up and dropped in the same carriage movement, but the carriage cannot hold 2 or more yarn carriers at the same time.


Press Off cannot cast off loops on the front upper needle bed.

Loops on the front upper needle bed must be cast off manually.



Other differences between MACH2X(S) and most shaping machines:

MACH2X(S) has no single global setting for takedown.

Each takedown device must be set individually.


MACH2X(S) has pulldown device.
MACH2X(S) has loop pressers, so it is suitable for knit structures with inlays or long floats.
MACH2X(S) has different Fixed Data specifications from shaping machines.

If you use the automatic option line drawing tool, it will generate fixed data settings based on shaping machine defaults. You must update these manually for MACH2X(S).


MACH2X(S) usually uses DSCS and i-DSCS.

Typically, this means that the size of the knitted loops is defined using loop length rather than stitch value.
Users must pay attention to loop length groups to ensure that the loop lengths are calculated in an appropriate manner.



Differences between MACH2X and MACH2XS:

MACH2X does not have movable sinkers. This makes it less reliable for partial knitting.
MACH2X does not have leading pull.

Leading pull is a feature where needles move down before moving up to catch new yarn. It is present on MACH2XS and some other Shima Seiki machines.

mach2x/dscs.title: DSCS
mach2x/dscs.content:
Mechanism
The DSCS encoder measures the actual length of yarn used and compares it with the theoretical length of yarn used. It then adjusts the stitch cams to keep the two lengths to within 0.5-1% of each other.
Threading
Thread the yarn through:

Top tension equipment.

Calibrate tension disk with an 8g weight.


DSCS encoder.
Both yarn sending rollers.
Tension disk between the yarn sending rollers.
Side tension arm.



Source: Page 6 of MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual.
Yarn angle control arm
Used when a larger length of yarn needs to be in contact with the encoder for it to spin correctly.
Use cases:

Knit structures with widely varying yarn lengths between different courses (e.g., jacquard, knit structures with many miss stitches or varying numbers of prolongations).
Slippery yarn.
Yarn with varying tension during knitting.


Source: Page 7 of MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual.
Knitting mode















































ModeStitch adj. update frequencyMinimum width for DSCS to functionRecommendationsControl 1 courseEvery course10-13”Control sum 1 roundEvery round3”For elastic yarns that will have a big tension difference between left-going and right-goingControl sum 1 courseEvery round, every few rounds, or every course, depending on fabric width3” for 1 round, 6” for 1 courseSamplingNo update (update only takes place during Compare mode)No minimum widthCompare (ALL)Update every garmentNo minimum widthCompare (PART)Sum 10m: update every 10m. Sum 30m: update every 30mNo minimum width
Need to press PREPA or RESET key before the changing the mode on the YARN MEASUREMENT screen.
Option line L9
The DSCS needs to be switched on to create or update stitch adjustment data, then switched off before the knit ends. This is done using L9=1, which acts as a toggle switch to change the DSCS state from on to off and vice versa. Each developed pattern must have an even number of =1, so that the DSCS is switched on and then switched off. (If you don’t need to use the DSCS, the developed pattern should not contain any =1 on L9).
Typically, =1 is placed at the first course of hem knitting to switch on the DSCS, and a second =1 is placed at the start of the end-of-pattern waste knitting to switch off the DSCS.
If you are knitting something that is likely to have high yarn errors, e.g., jacquard or bind off, you can use L9=2 on the relevant courses so that the DSCS ignores those courses.
The i-DSCS uses the same option line settings.

mach2x/fixed-data.title: Fixed Data
mach2x/fixed-data.content:
Fixed data for rib pattern
For MACH2XS, the main way to specify fixed data at the bottom of the developed pattern is:
!grid[0 1 0 2 0 1 0 2 / 0 1 0 2 0 3 0 4]
Note that the sequence starts from the leftmost !0 pixel, not the !1.
The upper row of the fixed data determines how the draw thread is knitted. In this example, !grid[0 1 0 2 0 1 0 2] specifies that the draw thread is knitted in half gauge.
Cast-off
Fixed data for the cast-off is a row of !3. This is the same as the fixed data for shaping machines.
Other notes
More information on how to draw fixed data can be found in SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > 3. Drawing Fixed Rib Data & 7. Changing Fixed Rib Data.
Credit to YH for the first version of these notes.

mach2x/front-body-back-body.title: Front Body Back Body
mach2x/front-body-back-body.content:
If you want more freedom to specify different knit structures on the front face and back face of the fabric, you can create 3 compressed patterns.

The first compressed pattern will be your ‘base’ pattern where the color numbers correspond to your package base patterns’ registration option line 1.
The second compressed pattern will be your front body pattern where you can draw the design that will be on the front face of the fabric.
The third compressed pattern will be your back body pattern where you can draw the design that will be on the back face of the fabric.

In Pattern Development, select WG Patt. Conversion (Y) (see X-Bed > Package Development for more details). Then, press the Area button to specify which compressed pattern represents the front body or back body, respectively.

Normal tab of Package Development dialogue box.
Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint.
R3 on bar
R3 on bar is used to specify whether a raster line 1 should be overwritten by the front body or back body. The following color numbers are used:

=10: Do not overwrite the original package base pattern.

Often used for lines that only specify transfers to ensure that the transfers are not overwritten.


=11…!110: Overwrite the original package base pattern.

Odd numbers reference the compressed pattern back body. =11 references the first line of the back body, =13 references the second line of the back body, etc.
Even numbers reference the compressed pattern front body. =12 references the first line of the front body, =14 references the second line of the front body, etc.
The following color numbers in the original package base pattern will not be overwritten:

Miss: !16/116/117.
Auto yarn feeder point: !13.
Pulldown pattern output code: !249/251/252/253/255.




=111..254: Overwrite the original package base pattern, but with a much larger set of color numbers that are not allowed to be overwritten. Use this when you want to be certain that tuck/move/transfer/etc. color numbers will not be overwritten.

Like before, odd numbers (=111/113/etc.) will reference the back body, while even numbers (=!112/114/etc.) will reference the front body.
Refer to SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > KnitPaint Help > Command on Option Line R3 Bar for the full list of color numbers in the original package base pattern that will not be overwritten.



Useful tools
Edit > Knit Edit tab > Knit Cancel Separation
Use this to remove rows on either the front bed or the back bed so that you can check if the front body/back body of the developed pattern is coming out as expected. The tool separates rows in the developed pattern based on option line color numbers.
Click on the small down arrow next to the icon with a white rectangle and a grey ‘flipping over’ arrow to select the front body or the back body.

Sync. Draw (upper toolbar)
Use this to select 3 compressed patterns to edit them simultaneously.

Footnotes


“Raster line” refers to a line of coloured pixels in KnitPaint (borrowing YH terminology). ↩

mach2x/loop-length-group.title: Loop Length Group
mach2x/loop-length-group.content:
Loop length
Wholegarment knitting usually specifies the amount of yarn for each loop using loop length (unit: mm) rather than stitch value. This is because the Wholegarment machines have devices to measure the length of yarn used and adjust the stitch cams so that the theoretical and actual lengths of yarn are similar. For example, if the actual length of yarn used to knit a course is more than the theoretical length of yarn that should be used, the stitch cams are adjusted using stitch adjustment data to reduce the needle actuation so that less yarn is pulled into each loop.
The machine switches from stitch value to loop length when the DSCS or i-DSCS mode is set to Control 1 Course, Control Sum, Sampling, or Compare (i.e., anything apart from Stitch).
If the yarn of a particular yarn carrier is not threaded through the DSCS or iDSCS, the loop length is translated to a stitch value automatically. Even if you specify the loop length, none of the stitch adjustment data or yarn error detection processes will apply.
Recommended loop lengths
For a 15L machine (see Needle), a Shima Seiki trainer recommended a loop length of 6.4mm.
Typically, the upper needle beds will use a smaller loop length than the lower needle beds to compensate for the loosening of the loop during the transfer between needle beds. The recommendation is 1mm smaller than the lower needle beds’ loop length, but do not make the loop length smaller than 4.8mm otherwise there will be insufficient yarn to form the loops.
Loop length group
Loop length groups determine:

How the theoretical loop length is measured.
How stitch adjustment data is updated during knitting.

Loop length group 1
Theoretical loop length excludes prolongations. Prolongations are the yarn that extends between the needle beds for knit structures with both front knits and back knits. For each prolongation, a constant value is added to the total length of yarn that should be used. The value of this constant is unknown even to the Shima Seiki trainers and technicians, and it is something that depends on the machine type and gauge.

Page 11 of MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual.
Group 1 is recommended for:

Knit structures without prolongations (e.g., single jersey).
Knit structures with a varying number of prolongations between courses.

By adding a constant value for every prolongation, that helps to account for the varying number of prolongations.
If the variation is extreme (e.g., jacquard), you may need to do a DSCS Ignore (L9=2) for the affected courses.



Loop length group 2
Theoretical loop length includes prolongations. Loop is defined as starting from the yarn that crosses the middle of the needle bed gap.

Page 11 of MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual.
Group 2 is recommended for:

Knit structures where the ratio between the number of stitches and the number of prolongations is constant (e.g., rib, interlock).

If the ratio is not consistent, do not use Group 2 because the i-DSCS will try to use the same total theoretical yarn length for every course, so courses with more prolongations will have tighter loops, and courses with fewer prolongations will have looser loops.

Page 12 of MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual.
Loop length group 3
I don’t use this because I don’t use Sampling/Compare mode. Read the manual instead.
Loop length group 4
Stitch adjustment data is not created or updated. Uses stitch mode and stitch value table, even though the user might still be manipulating the loop length table rather than the stitch value table.
Group 4 is recommended for:

Setup
Bind off

Loop length subgroups
Each loop length group and subgroup stores its own stitch adjustment data. If you are using different knit structures when knitting with the same yarn carrier, use different loop length groups and subgroups so that the stitch adjustment data can be updated independently for each group to avoid large differences between the theoretical and actual amounts of yarn that are used (i.e., yarn errors). Specify which loop length group/subgroup to use on option line R6.
Examples:

Use loop length group 2a for rib, and loop length group 2b for interlock.
Use loop length group 1a for single jersey, and loop length group 1b for single jersey with cables.


Source: Page 10 of MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual.

mach2x/loop-routine.title: Loop Routine
mach2x/loop-routine.content:
Calibrates the Stitch Adjustment Data to match desired loop lengths before the knitting program is started (vs. on-the-fly adjustment that i-DSCS does automatically, which may take a while to settle and result in inconsistent appearance across different portions of the knitted fabric).
Upload the .000 for your actual knitting programme so that the machine knows which yarn carriers to do loop routine for.
Required width of yarn

If using i-DSCS , 6” width is ok.
If using DSCS, ≥10” is needed when using Control 1 Course mode.

Parameters

Mode:

INDEPEND: Will knit a flat panel.
INDEPENDWG: Will knit a tube.

Default is to knit 3 tubes (as if knitting a garment).
If only 1 tube is needed, only list the yarn carrier number for M so that only the middle tube is knitted.


SEQUENTIAL: Will start knitting your actual programme after finishing loop routine.


Loose loop.

The loop length of the course just before the transfer (e.g., transfer from front bed to back bed to test different needle beds).

A looser stitch makes the transfer easier.


However, if the loop length is large, the stitch cam will force the needle to move a longer distance, which may cause the yarn to break.
Recommended loop lengths: Make rib loose loop length tight (e.g., 6.0mm), SJ loose loop length can be 6.8mm.

Rib loose loop length uses loop length group 2, so the loop length is inclusive of the prolongation.
Rib structure is stressful on the yarn because the yarn is pulled from the front and back needle beds simultaneously to form the rib structure.

Therefore, reduce the loop length to reduce how much the yarn is pulled.






Stitch adjustment clear.

ON by default. All previous stitch adjustment data is cleared.
If using a similar/same yarn as the previous job, selecting OFF will save time and yarn, because the previous stitch adjustment data is re-used.


When “EY” (elastic yarn) is selected, loop routine does “round mode.”

Right-going and left-going yarn tensions will have very different tension when using elastic yarn, so doing Control 1 Course will be inappropriate because of the vastly different tensions depending on the carriage direction.

Pushing direction will tend to have larger loops.
Pulling direction will tend to have smaller loops.

mach2x/needle.title: Needle
mach2x/needle.content:
The MACH2X M173X15L has 15L needles.

15 gauge spacing (15 needles an inch).
Large needle hook (similar to 12 gauge needle hook?).
Compound needles (a.k.a. slide needles).

Hook (slide needle) and transfer prongs (slider) can be purchased separately.


Number of needles:

1.7m wide: 1020 needles per bed.
1.5m wide: 900 needles per bed.

mach2x/option-lines.title: Option Lines
mach2x/option-lines.content:
These option lines are particularly important.
Left side option lines:

L5: Speed (knitting)
L6: Speed (transfer)
L7: Yarn adjustment, carriage adjustment, pause
L9: DSCS on/off/ignore.

Needs two =1s


L10: Pulldown (knitting).
L11: Pulldown (transfer).
L13: Used bed.
L16: Pulldown device pattern.

Typically =3, needs to be set in Auto Process Parameters > Pulldown tab.



Right side option lines:

R1: Jump economizer.
R3: Yarn carrier.
R5: Loop length/stitch value.
R11: Stitch presser.

=1 to activate STP.
=4 to deactivate STP.


R18: Loop presser.

=1 to activate LP.



These option lines may come in handy sometimes:

R4: Knit system specification.

=16/17: N line 1 system knit.
Other color numbers allow you to knit using specific systems.

mach2x/package-pattern-gather-up.title: Package Pattern Gather Up
mach2x/package-pattern-gather-up.content:
Package > Package Pat. Gather Up is used to retrieve package base patterns within the Shima Seiki database.
I rarely use it so I’m not completely confident of the steps.

mach2x/press-off.title: Press Off
mach2x/press-off.content: Press off knitting cannot cast off needles on the front upper (FU) needle bed. Any loops on the FU bed need to be cast off manually before doing press off knitting.

mach2x/pulldown-device.title: Pulldown Device
mach2x/pulldown-device.content:
The pulldown device (PDD) is a claw-like device that pulls on the knitted fabric to provide takedown force. It is located between the subroller and the main/exit roller. Each PDD block is 1.5” wide on the MACH2XS. On a 15 gauge machine, each PDD block will span about 23 needles. There are two rows of PDD blocks, one on the back and one on the front.

Yellow highlighted area shows the activated pulldown devices.
Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Lecture Help > 2. Pulldown Device > Interval.
Advantages:

Can provide effective takedown force because it is quite close to the needle bed gap.
Can provide differentiated takedown force across the width of the fabric.

Disadvantages:

The downward-facing pins can puncture silicone tubes.

Mechanism
To pull down the fabric, the PDD tilts towards the fabric. The downward-facing metal pins catch onto the fabric and pull the fabric down.
PDD parameters
Always set the speed of the rotating metal shaft to 1000rpm.
PDD position
“Position” refers to the stroke length of the PDD. A longer stroke length will correspond to greater force.
Stroke length for MACH2XS (not sure about MACH2X):

Weak: 7mm drop, a spring pulls the PDD up to reduce the drop force.
Medium: 12mm drop. PDD drops using self-weight.
Strong: 12mm drop. PDD drops using self-weight plus additional force from an extra spring.

Weak or Medium positions are suitable for most fabrics.
PDD interval
“Interval” refers to the number of courses before the PDD activates. Courses are counted in terms of carriage moves, so a knit cancel course will still count as a course.
To make the pulldown force very weak, on the knitting machine screen, set the box next to the number of courses per interval to “X”. Once the PDD drops to its lowest position, it will pause and will not move or release. This is useful for bind off where many courses/carriage moves are made but hardly any new fabric is created, so you want the PDD to hold the fabric without pulling it down.
The PDD blocks are grouped as sets of 4 blocks. The blocks do not all move at the same time. Instead, they are activated in the following sequence: block 1, block 3, block 2, block 4.

Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Lecture Help > 2. Pulldown Device > Pulldown Position.
Usage notes
Changing the PDD position results in a more marked change in takedown force. Changing the PDD interval results in a more subtle change in takedown force.
Can think of it as:

“Position” is amplitude.
“Interval” is wavelength or period.

Option lines
Option lines L10 (knitting) and L11 (transfer)
Typical color numbers:

Waste knitting after setup: L10=3, L11=13.
Body fabric: L10=4, L11=14.

The takedown settings associated with each color number are specified in Knitting Adjust.
For L11, typically specify a weaker setting than L10 since no new fabric is being created.
If carriage system 2 is knitting during a given carriage movement, then the L10 settings will be used even if transfers are done in the same carriage movement.
Option line L16 Pulldown Pattern
The color number on L16 is an index. The actual pulldown pattern for each index is set in Auto Process Parameters > Pulldown tab.

Meaning of each numbered pulldown pattern. Remember that this applies to the number specified in Auto Process Parameters > Pulldown tab, and does not apply to the color number on the developed pattern’s option line.
Source: KnitPaint > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > Option Lines > L16: Pulldown Pattern > 1-80.
Meaning of different PDD actions:

Set: PDD is moving.

Short stroke means a 12mm PDD stroke.
Normal set with stroke length 24mm is not supported for MACH2XS 15 gauge, but may be available for other knitting machines (e.g. 8 gauge).


Pause: PDD holds the fabric without moving down, but has a small open-close action at intervals.

Useful during bind off to prevent fabric from rising and piling up.


Release/open: PDD opens up so that it is not holding the fabric.

Pulldown pattern =7.
Release may be useful to aid transfers, e.g., when joining a vertically knitted part to a horizontal part (e.g., special neck, joining top of sleeve to shoulder).



Option line L18 Pulldown Pattern Adjustment
Adjusts the number of PDD blocks that are used.
Auto Process Parameters Pulldown tab
SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > 5. Automatic Software Settings and 6. Auto Process Parameters has a lot of helpful information.

Pulldown pattern

Outside set: Outside the knitting area.

For most fabrics, specify pattern 0 (F/B pause).


Set: Inside the knitting area.

Note that “set” here has a different meaning from “set” referring to a PDD action. (Isn’t it confusing?)
For most fabrics, specify pattern 10 (F/B set short stroke).
When knitting on only the back (e.g., at the back neckline of a sweater), you may want to use patter 12 (F release, B set short stroke).



Mirror process

Take down tension is more stable if PDD pattern is symmetrical.

Every time the number of PDD blocks in use changes, all the PDDs reset to the original uppermost position.
Without mirror process, the number of times the number of PDD blocks changes is larger, so there are many more PDD resets.


Don’t make the PDD pattern symmetrical if the knit itself is not symmetrical.
The line of reflection is where !10 is drawn on the assignment line.

If you need to knit off-centre, on the assignment line, draw !10 to specify the centre of the needle bed and !110 to specify the line of reflection.
It is not possible to have multiple lines of reflection in a single knit.



% of output
This specifies when a PDD block will be activated. If x% of the needles within the width of a PDD block are active, then the PDD block will be activated. Typically set to 20%.
Complement and erasing course
When the number of active needles changes, the number of active pulldown blocks may change. Every time the number of active pulldown blocks changes, all the PDD blocks to reset to their original uppermost position. Complement course and erasing course are used to avoid unnecessary PDD block resets.
Complement course
If there are parts of the pulldown pattern visualisation (see Auto Process Parameters > Pulldown tab > Preview) where the number of active PDD blocks decreases for a few courses, KnitPaint can ‘fill in’ the deactivated PDD blocks so that the PDD blocks that would otherwise be deactivated remain active, so that the number of active PDD blocks does not change. The specified number of complement courses indicates the threshold at/below which the !0 courses (i.e., PDD front pause, back pause) will be filled in. The recommended value is 10 courses.
Erasing course
If there are parts of the pulldown pattern visualisation where the number of active PDD blocks increases for a few courses, KnitPaint can ‘erase’ those active PDD blocks so that the number of active PDD blocks does not change. The recommended default threshold is 2 courses.
Erasing course only takes effect when 1 pulldown block is affected.
Shift knit course
This setting takes effect when !249 is used in the developed pattern (e.g., for garments with sleeve and body knitting ranges that slide to connect). Shift Knit Course is used to shift the pulldown pattern upwards by a specified number of courses so that the pulldown pattern specified for a particular course takes effect when that particular course is (approximately) in physical contact with the pulldown device. This is to compensate for the fact that the pulldown device is located some distance below the needle bed gap (where knitting is actually taking place), and the loops have to descend by 100-150 courses before they are actually in contact with the pulldown device.
Knit cancel
This instructs KnitPaint on what pulldown pattern to use when there are idle needles holding loops.
On the package base patterns and developed pattern, typically, specify !255 for needles that are idle but still holding loops so that knit cancel courses are assigned a pulldown pattern.
Alternatively, use !251/252/253 to specify different pulldown patterns for different areas with idle needles holding loops.
Viewing and manually editing the pulldown pattern
Press the Preview button in Auto Process Parameters > Pulldown tab to view the pulldown pattern visualisation.
I am slightly less confident of these instructions to manually edit the pulldown pattern because I almost never use .tdd files.

In Automatic Software Settings.

Select “output pulldown data.”
Select “auto draw of pulldown open/close” and “open/close 2.”
Select “auto process pattern development.”


Press [1,2,3,4] button on right side of KnitPaint screen.

Data select:

Mode: Load.

Opens pattern data and pulldown data as .000 files.






On the pulldown data, modify the pulldown data manually (e.g., draw “7” to release PDD).

It is better to make the horizontal extent of your drawing match where the PDD blocks start and end.

If your drawing doesn’t match, KnitPaint will automatically modify the pulldown pattern data, and you may get unexpected outcomes.


Use the Composite function to overlap the pattern data and pulldown data to see where to modify the pulldown data.


To save the manual changes:

Press [1,2,3,4] button.

Data select: pulldown data.
Mode: save (normal).
Knitting machine: (choose your machine model).
Execute.

Select pattern area.
Pulldown is saved as a .tdd file.






To load the .tdd file on the knitting machine:

Load .999 file.
Load .000 file.
Load .tdd file.

Load this last to overwrite any pulldown data created during ASS.




To view .tdd on KnitPaint.
[1,2,3,4] button.

Data select: pulldown data.
Mode: load.

Dialogue box: Click “data select” then select .tdd file to open.





Tips
Very occasionally, a knit turns out badly because of the position of the fabric relative to the PDD. E.g., the fabric may be positioned so that a few loops on the left side overlap with a PDD block, while the number of loops on the right side are too few to activate the PDD block, causing the left side to have excessive takedown force and the right side to have insufficient takedown force. Shifting the position of the fabric on the needle bed can help to even out the PDD force.

mach2x/ssd.title: SSD
mach2x/ssd.content:
Suggested files to store on the SSD:

.999 files for Knitting Adjust settings for different fabric widths/etc.
.000 files to test the needle beds for broken needles.
.000 and .SEQ files for sequential knitting.

mach2x/starting-and-ending.title: Starting and Ending
mach2x/starting-and-ending.content:
Starting
Since the MACH2X is usually used for seamless Wholegarment knitting, you may want to create a setup knitting structure (after the fixed data) that will not unravel even after the draw thread is removed.
It can be a lot easier to adjust the takedown settings by knitting a long piece of waste fabric until the comb releases and the takedown is handled by the pulldown device and main/exit roller. To do so, you can create a programme that knits waste yarn using jump economizer (for easy editing of the jump economizer value), followed by a course (or two courses) of draw thread to separate the waste yarn courses from the actual knitted item. On the MACH2X173-15L, typically the pulldown device is activated after 80-90 waste yarn courses, and the comb is released and the main/exit roller is activated after 134-150 waste yarn courses.
Ending
The fixed data for cast-off will only cast off loops from the front lower needle bed (FD). Loops on any other beds will need to be cast off or transferred to to the front lower needle bed before specifying !3 for cast-off fixed data.

mach2x/stitch-adjustment-data.title: Stitch Adjustment Data
mach2x/stitch-adjustment-data.content:
MACH2X DSCS Instruction Manual
DSCS = Digital Stitch Control System.
Page 5:
The DSCS adjusts the position of the stitch cams so that the difference between the preset and actual loop length becomes within ±1% or ±0.5%. (You can switch between ±1% and ±0.5% on the operation screen. 0.5% is more accurate but will result in a longer Loop Routine) The data for this adjustment is memorized in the controller. The data is called “stitch adjustment data.”
Stitch adjustment data is created during loop routine and is updated during knitting, but the timing of the update depends on the mode.





























ModeUpdate frequencyControl 1 courseEvery courseControl sumEvery round or every course, depending on setting and fabric widthSamplingNo update (update only takes place during Compare mode)Compare (ALL)Update every garmentCompare (PART)Sum 10m: update every 10m. Sum 30m: update every 30m

mach2x/takedown.title: Takedown
mach2x/takedown.content:
The MACH2X has 4 types of takedown devices:

Comb.
Subroller.
Pulldown Device.
Main/exit roller.


Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Lecture Help > 2. Pulldown Device > Interval.
Unlike the shaping machines, there is no overall value to control all of the takedown devices. (I think Stoll machines also have an overall value?)

mach2x/threading.title: Threading
mach2x/threading.content:
Yarn tension assembly
Top yarn tension arm (with yarn removed) should be adjusted to 8g. Adjust to an even larger force if needed, e.g., for thick yarns or inlay knitting).
Tension equipment (tension disk)
Adjust tension disk using 8g weight if the yarn is threaded through the i-DSCS or DSCS.
Adjust tension disk using 3g weight if the yarn is not threaded through the i-DSCS or DSCS.
Effect on yarn tension
The calibration weight of the tension disk and the  yarn sending rollers can make considerable differences to the stitch density of the fabric.
Samples threaded through the i-DSCS tend to come out larger, suggesting a looser yarn tension due to the yarn sending device.
Yarn carrier
If the yarn carrier has a roller, threading through the roller is supposed to be better than threading through the pink ceramic eyelet.
Tying up
Suggestion is to use a slip knot to tie up any unwanted yarns for easy removal.
If the yarn carrier has a roller, place the loop of the slip knot over both the pink ceramic eyelet and the roller. This ensures that the loop stays open.

mach2x/x-bed.title: X-Bed
mach2x/x-bed.content:
“X-bed” refers to a four needle bed flat knitting machine configuration.
”V-bed” refers to a two needle bed configuration. In reality, the two needle beds are in an inverted V-shape configuration (Ʌ).
In a similar way, for an X-bed configuration, the four needle beds are not in an X-shape configuration. Instead, the configuration is more like two inverted V’s stacked on top of each other (/Ʌ\).
The four needle beds are:

Front lower (FD - front down)
Front upper (FU - that’s what Shima Seiki calls it)
Back lower (BD - back down)
Back upper (BU)

The X-bed configuration allows you to knit full gauge knit structures that require both front and back needle beds (e.g., tubular structures, double-layer fabrics) AND transfers (e.g., inside shaping, knit structures that require back knits on the front bed/front knits on the back bed). This is because the empty upper needle beds can be used to transfer loops. Most Wholegarment patterns are knitted as tubes, which is what makes the X-bed configuration helpful.

Images showing how a 2x2 rib tube uses the BU needle bed to do back knits for the front face.
Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Lecture Help > 6. Basic Knitting of WG > 2x2 Rib.
Topologically 1, any knit structure that can be knitted on an X-bed machine can be knitted on a V-bed machine, although it may require half gauge or 1x1 knitting so that there are empty needles to handle transfers and links-links knit structures without disrupting the tube structure.
Needle bed limitations

Needle beds cannot do all-needle knitting.
Upper needle beds cannot do tucks.
If a loop is held on the upper needle bed, knitting cannot take place on the lower needle bed directly below the loop.

E.g., if a loop is held on BU needle 10, the loop will block BD needle 10 from being used.



These limitations apply to the MACH2X and MACH2XS machines that I have used. I am not sure if they apply to newer machines (e.g., SWG-XR).
Transfer rules
Loops can be transferred between the following needle beds:

FD and BD (front lower, back lower).
FD and BU (front lower, back upper).
BD and FU (back lower, front upper).

Loops cannot be transferred between the following needle beds:

FU and BU (front upper, back upper).
FD and FU (front lower, front upper).
BD and BU (back lower, back upper).


Side view of the four needle beds, with yellow highlights showing the permissible transfers between needle beds.
Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Lecture Help > 4. Action of Each Part on Machine > Four Needle Beds.
Option lines
More information on each option line can be found in KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help.
L13
Option line L13 is used to specify which needle beds are used for knitting. Using the wrong specifications on L13 will probably lead to unexpected outcomes, e.g., knitting a flat panel instead of a tube.
Most common L13 specifications:

=0: Use FD and BD.
=81: Use FD and BU (compulsive transfer).
=82: Use BD and FU (compulsive transfer).
=31: Use FD and BU.
=32: Use BD and FU.

L13=0 is used when you want to knit using only the lower needle beds, e.g., when knitting an interlock fabric.
L13=81 and =82 are used when you want to knit a double-layer structure that needs inside shaping or back knits on the front face (and vice versa).
For example, if you want to knit a tube with rib knit structure, use =81 to knit the front face and =82 to knit the back face. =81 will knit the front knits on FD and the back knits on BU, then the back knits will be transferred from BU to FD. =82 will knit the back knits on BD and the front knits on FU, then the front knits will be transferred from FU to BD. =81/82 have ‘compulsive transfer’, which means that auto-transfer will be performed with carriage systems S1 and S3.
L13=31/32 are similar to =81/82, but =31/32 will not perform auto-transfer with S1/S3 when =31/32 are placed continuously. This reduces the number of transfers and may reduce the chance of loops dropping or otherwise malfunctioning during transfers.
Refer to SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > 2. Option Line > L13: Used Bed for more details.
R9
Sometimes, you need to explicitly tell KnitPaint to not do auto transfers or links process to ensure that your knit structure is knitted as intended.
Most common R9 specifications:

=1: Links process ignore.
=11: (When selecting WG) S1 and S3; auto-transfer process ignore..

Refer to SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > 2. Option Line > R9: Links Process Ignore for more details.
R5
If you want to do transfers using !20/29/30/39 without knitting, you can also use the following R5 option line settings together with knit + transfer color numbers:

=30: Knit cancel, use FD and BD for transfers.
=31: Knit cancel, use FD and BU for transfers.
=32: Knit cancel, use BD and FU for transers.

Admittedly, I have not used this before. I always use R5=1 together with L13 to specify which needle beds to use for transfers.
Refer to SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > 2. Option Line > R5: Knit Cancel for more details.
Knit out of commanded bed
If you have a course in your package base pattern that needs to use three needle beds, use the following ‘out of commanded bed’ (OoCB) color numbers in the structure area, along with L13.

!114: Front knit (out of commanded bed) (without links process).
!115: Back knit (out of commanded bed) (without links process).

For example, if you want to knit using FD, BU, and BD, use L13=81 to specify that FD and BU should be used. But where you need to knit on BD, use !115 to specify a back knit out of the commanded bed. I.e., the L13 command is to use BU, but !115 uses BD instead.
Sometimes, Shima Seiki patterns use L13=81/82 and !1/2/114/115 to knit interlock, instead of using L13=0 and !51/52.
Refer to SDS-ONE KnitPaint > Help > Automatic Software Help > MACH2X/MACH2XS > 1. Color No. List for more details.
Package development
Since tubular fabrics require a course on the back needle bed and a course on the front needle bed to form 1 complete round, a tubular fabric that is 100 courses tall in real life will require a developed pattern that is 200 courses tall (100 courses on the back bed, 100 courses on the front bed). If you prefer to draw compressed patterns that are the same ‘height’ as the fabric will be in real life, in the Package Development dialogue box, select:

Normal tab
Compose section: WG patt. conversion
Conversion direction: Y


Normal tab of Package Development dialogue box.
Source: SDS-ONE KnitPaint.
If this is selected, during package development, every line of the compressed pattern will be duplicated so that the compressed pattern becomes twice as tall before replacing the compressed pattern with the package base patterns. But this means that registration option line 2 2 needs to specify twice the the number of lines too, so that the package base patterns are correctly inserted into the compressed pattern.

Example showing how the compressed pattern is doubled in height, and therefore registration option line 2 must match the doubled compressed pattern.
Source: SDS-One KnitPaint > Help > KnitPaint Help > 2. Registration Option Line (Paint).
Specifying WG patt. conversion (Y) also allows you to use the Package Development > Normal tab > Position section > Area tool to select separate compressed patterns for the front body and back body (see Front Body Back Body for more details).
Are you confused yet?
Footnotes


“Topologically” is used in the sense of, considering only the invariant spatial relationships, and not the geometry or dimensions. ↩


Registration option line 2 specifies the number of lines in the compressed pattern that correspond with the package base pattern. For example, if registration option line 2 =2, 2 lines in the compressed pattern will be replaced with all the lines in the package base pattern to form the developed pattern. If WG patt. conversion (Y) is selected, the number of lines in the compressed pattern are counted after doubling the compressed pattern. Refer to SDS-One KnitPaint > Help > KnitPaint Help > 2. Registration Option Line (Paint) for more details. ↩

mach2x/yarn-error.title: Yarn Error
mach2x/yarn-error.content:
YARN ERR is a threshold setting on the YARN MEASUREMENT screen. It compares the reference (theoretical) yarn amount against the actual measured yarn amount . When the difference exceeds the percentage you’ve set, the machine stops with an error.
The manuals advice setting Yarn Error to 10% for Control mode.
(I usually use 15% to avoid errors.)
If a Yarn Error occurs during knitting, check if there is something wrong with the yarn path (e.g., yarn slipped out of encoder) or the fabric (e.g., yarn breakage at the needle bed). If everything seems ok, you can try increasing the Yarn Error threshold to continue knitting.
Structures with a lot of yarn length variations (e.g., jacquard) may have a lot of yarn errors. In such a situation, try using L9=2 (DSCS ignore). If you are already knitting and the yarn carrier with errors is threaded through the i-DSCS, try changing the i-DSCS mode to something that does not update the stitch adjustment data (e.g., PLT OFF).

mach2x/i-dscs.title: i-DSCS
mach2x/i-dscs.content:
The i-DSCS and DSCS use the same option line settings for L9.
Mechanism
The i-DSCS+DTC is the only ‘active’ yarn sending system on the MACH2X (excluding any additional accessories to the machine). The yarn is gripped between a driving pulley and driven pulley. Based on feedback from the buffer arm angle, the driving pulley spins to send yarn towards the yarn carrier to maintain a stable yarn tension. For example, if the buffer arm angle is low, that suggests that the yarn is tight, so the driving pulley spins to send out more yarn to loosen the tension until the buffer arm returns to a horizontal position.

Source: Page 4 of i-DSCS+DTC Instruction Manual.

Source: Page 11 of i-DSCS+DTC Instruction Manual.
Threading
Thread the yarn through:

Top tension equipment.

Calibrate tension disk with an 8g weight.


i-DSCS.


Source: Page 5 of i-DSCS+DTC Instruction Manual.
To make it easier to pull the yarn through, use Manual Machine Operation > Yarn Sending ON.
Yarn considerations
Do not:

Feed the set-up yarn and draw thread.
Use the yarn sending device (i.e., side roller) and side tension arm.
Feed 3 or more yarns through the i-DSCS because the large number of yarns may drop out of the pulley.

3rd yarn should skip the i-DSCS and use the yarn sending device (i.e., side roller) and side tension arm instead.



Based on personal experience, yarns with high bending stiffness (e.g., thick monofilaments) may not ‘flow’ through the buffer arm smoothly. I tried threading 0.3mm nylon monofilament through the i-DSCS and when the yarn was tight, the driving pulley spun to send yarn, but because the yarn didn’t move through the eyelet of the buffer arm, the buffer arm angle didn’t change so that driving pulley ended up sending a massive tangle of yarn.
Dynamic Tension Control (DTC)
DTC changes the tension of the buffer arm depending on the yarn sending speed.
Knitting mode

Sum 30m: update every 30mNo minimum width
Need to press PREPA or RESET key before the changing the mode on the YARN MEASUREMENT screen.
Mode for each yarn carrier















































ModeWhat it doesStitch Adj. Updated?When to useWEAKYarn sending active, normal tension.✅ YesDefault for all normal yarn carriers. Start here.MEDIUMHigher buffer arm tension than WEAK.✅ YesIf yarn sags/slacks with WEAK setting.STRONGEven higher tension.✅ YesIf yarn still sags with MEDIUM.ELA. Table generated by Claude.ai, mostly based on page 38 of i-DSCS+DTC Instruction Manual.
Weak/Medium/Strong/etc. are presets with default values for the buffer arm tension (unit: gf) for different speeds. If necessary, the buffer arm tension can be changed manually.

Maximum: 40gf
Minimum: 3gf

0gf means that the i-DSCS is not being used

The example below shows that the buffer arm tension is set to a higher force at a low knitting speed.

Source: Page 39 of i-DSCS+DTC Instruction Manual.
The only time I have seen the buffer arm tension being adjusted is during training in Wakayama, when the plating was not stable. In the end, a trainer found that setting the main yarn to a very high tension and the plating yarn to a very low tension made the plating more stable (but it still wasn’t perfect).
Troubleshooting

Yarn Error.

Check if the threading is ok, e.g., if the yarn slipped out from the driving/driven pulleys or if the yarn is stuck somewhere.
Check if there is yarn breakage at the needle bed.
Check if your pattern has a lot of variation in yarn length between courses.
Check if the yarn is so thin that is is slipping between the driving/driven pulleys. If yes, try changing the textured rubber to a smooth rubber to improve contact between the yarn and the pulleys.


Yarn breakage detected by buffer arm.

Check if the yarn broke.
If there seems to be no issue with the yarn, check if the buffer arm angle tends to be on the high side. If yes, try increasing the i-DSCS force (e.g., from W to M).

With elastic yarn, sometimes I find that W mode works better than ELA. YARN mode. ELA. YARN mode seemed to make the yarn tension too weak.

mach2x/index.title: MACH2X for Shima Seiki Shaping Machine Users
mach2x/index.content:
These are (informal) notes about the Shima Seiki MACH2X knitting machine. The notes assume that the reader is familiar with Shima Seiki shaping machines and the Package Base Pattern → Compressed Pattern → Developed Pattern workflow.
You’ll get more accurate information from the Shima Seiki manuals 1 and help files. So, the purpose of these notes is to (1) highlight concepts and settings that I find more relevant when using the MACH2X, (2) explain the concepts in the way that I understand them, (3) include tips from my experience with the machines, and (4) record things that I keep on forgetting.

notes-to-selves.title: Notes to Selves
notes-to-selves.content:
Formatting

Title case for page titles. Sentence case for all other headings.
No empty line between heading and body text.
Use ## Level 2 Headings for top level organization within notes - common convention inherited from HTML where <h1> represents the page title, rendered separately from ‘body’ content. Child headings use ### h3 and so on. tip keyboard shortcut Ctrl-Alt-[number]  to change heading levels directly

Spelling

“Color number” uses American spelling to follow Shima Seiki spelling.
Are “full gauge” and “half gauge” supposed to be hyphenated?
Lean towards numerals rather than spelling out numbers.

Presumably numerals are easier for non-native English speakers to understand.



Punctuation

Put full stops at the end of bullet points.

Phrasing

Is there a concise way to say “knitting the back stitch for the front body or the front stitch for the back body?” The quote is from the Shima Seiki Automatic Software Help page for option line L13.

Thoughts on Documentation

”In your carpet bag, carry a large shawl, and if you will travel by night, or stop where it will be inconvenient to open your trunks, carry your night clothes, and what clean linen you may require, in the carpet bag. It is best to have your name and address engraved upon the plate of your carpet bag, and to sew a white card, with your name and the address to which you are traveling, in clear, plain letters upon it. If you carry a novel or any other reading, it is best to carry the book in your satchel, and not open the carpet bag until you are ready for the night. If you are to pass the night in the cars, carry a warm woolen or silk hood, that you may take off your bonnet at night. No one can sleep comfortably in a bonnet. Carry also, in this case, a large shawl to wrap round your feet.”
